strengths: R2E offers a coherent contribution to retrieval-based NLP: representing candidate answers through masked evidence enables quantitative attribution of the Reasoner’s score to individual passages. Training with a learned NULL representation makes the Shapley interventions better aligned with training conditions.

The experiments support useful performance without sacrificing inspectability. Uncorrected R2E improves Gene Description Facts MRR over MCS (0.202 versus 0.176), while literature-based R2E achieves clinical-outcome AUROC comparable to MLM (0.632 versus 0.630). Using templated genetics, R2E improves over the ontology-based genetics baseline (0.579 versus 0.545).

The literature experiments include meaningful safeguards and controls: document-level splits, temporal restrictions, training from scratch to avoid pretrained-model leakage, architectural ablations, and evidence-corpus updates without retraining. The genetics comparison also includes a restricted evaluation on diseases with genetic insight.

The three released benchmarks and detailed architecture, training, attribution, and prompting specifications provide a useful community contribution and support methodological reimplementation. The supported retrieval-and-attribution contribution warrants Findings consideration.
weaknesses: Evidence for scientifically useful explanations remains limited. Shapley attribution explains the fixed Reasoner relative to its NULL baseline, but does not establish that the model reasons correctly about biology. Clinical evidence relevance reaches only 0.665 AUROC against GPT-4 labels. Human validation involves one expert and eight query-target pairs per task, without inter-annotator reliability or a decision-support study. The auditing experiment also lacks a matched random-selection or retrieval-similarity control to establish the benefit of selecting evidence through Shapley values.

The clinical benchmark supports narrower conclusions than confirmed therapeutic efficacy. Appendix P treats discontinued Phase II/III development as failure and pre-registration or later stages as success. Commercial decisions, safety, and molecule-specific problems can confound these labels, as the authors acknowledge. Furthermore, the pre-2005 restriction applies to literature; the 2024 genetics dataset and GPT-4 auditing are not demonstrated to respect that cutoff. The combined and audited variants therefore require qualification as retrospective evaluations.

Some performance gains are insufficiently isolated. Frequency correction substantially improves balanced ranking results, but the MLM baseline is not given the analogous correction explicitly derived in Appendix G. A genetics-only semantic-similarity baseline would help separate the contribution of the Reasoner from improved disease-term matching. The small clinical gains from combining modalities and auditing would also benefit from uncertainty estimates that account for repeated targets/diseases and training variability.

Exact empirical replication is constrained by the proprietary corpus and entity-linking pipeline, with neither code nor model weights released. The extensive methodological description supports reimplementation, but the public evaluation datasets alone cannot reconstruct the training data or retrieval indices. An executable reproduction using an accessible corpus would substantially strengthen verifiability.

Appendix F contains a mathematical mismatch: Section 3.4 samples negatives uniformly while excluding the true entity, whereas the derivation assumes a query-independent uniform distribution over all entities. Under the stated sampler, the negative conditional probability is proportional to 1 minus the positive conditional probability. Consequently, the exact log-probability and PMI interpretations require correction or an explicit approximation; the empirically useful frequency correction can still be presented as a heuristic.
